claims.text: Premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by differential elemental segregation driven by local surface-energy and melting-point disparities.
Copper has a lower melting point than the other constituent elements relevant to the proposed transition.
Copper preferentially segregates to the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Surface-segregated copper forms the initial liquid-like layer.
A Cu-rich liquid-like surface layer reduces the cohesive stability of the nanoparticle core.
Reduced core cohesion caused by the Cu-rich layer triggers inward progression toward bulk melting.
Sub-surface enrichment in Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co temporarily retards complete melting because these elements have higher surface energies.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions and are likely FCC.
The relevant structural mediator is a Cu-enriched surface layer adjacent to a sub-surface region relatively enriched in Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co.
Copper migrates to the surface because of its lower dissolution potential and surface energy.
A liquid layer at the surface creates a phase boundary that allows a melting front to advance inward.
The Cu-rich liquid-like surface layer appears below the bulk melting point.
Melting initiates at the nanoparticle periphery rather than uniformly throughout the particle.
Complete melting is delayed by stabilization from the Fe-, Ni-, Cr-, and Co-enriched sub-surface region.
An inert atmosphere precludes oxidation during the heating experiment.
Extremely rapid heating may permit stress-induced melting to dominate over the proposed segregation mechanism.
Oxidizing environments may permit oxidation-driven phase changes to dominate over the proposed segregation mechanism.
Pre-inducing Cu surface enrichment should alter the onset of surface premelting relative to initially homogeneous particles if Cu segregation drives the transition.
